items.headline: NASA seeks only ‘good deal’ international partners, pauses Lunar Gateway
items.title: Isaacman Doubles Down on New NASA Model for International Partnerships
items.scifi_hook: NASA tells allies it will only join space coalitions that benefit the US.
items.eli5: NASA will only work with other countries if the partnership is clearly advantageous.
items.why: Ensures U.S. retains strategic advantage in lunar exploration.
items.text: HOUSTON, TX — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is less than a year on the job, but he’s already upended the way the agency interacts with the rest of the world. NASA doesn’t want to go it alone as it drives a US-led effort to return American astronauts to the Moon. But the agency is done “stitch[ing] together coalitions for the sake of coalitions,” Isaacman said at Payload’s Off World event in Houston on Wednesday. The comments come one week after Isaacman made similar remarks at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference, saying that NASA was only interested in international partnerships that were “good deals” for the US. Trial separation: Together, the comments highlight the increasingly strained relationship between the US and European civil space programs since Isaacman took the top job at NASA. Isaacman’s appointment was quickly followed by NASA’s decision to pause work on the Lunar Gateway program—a program where ESA had already invested in and started building three main components. That pause kickstarted a rift between the two agencies, which has only grown wider in the months since. It reached a new zenith this month when ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher called on European leaders to decide whether the region should forge its own capabilities on space exploration. items.headline: Rainbow Rare Earths secures Neo offtake for Phalaborwa project
items.title: Rainbow Rare Earths deal with Neo clears path for Phalaborwa study
items.scifi_hook: South Africa’s new rare‑earth mine will ship processed material to a Canadian tech firm.
items.eli5: Rainbow will sell 40% of its neodymium‑praseodymium output to Neo, which will help design the extraction plant.
items.why: Locks in market for rare‑earths needed in clean‑energy magnets.
items.text: Rainbow Rare Earths (LON: RBW) has cleared a key technical hurdle at its Phalaborwa rare earths project in South Africa through an offtake and processing agreement with Neo Performance Materials (TSX: NEO), paving the way for a prefeasibility study (PFS) in the fourth quarter. The memorandum of understanding gives Toronto-based Neo offtake rights to 40% of Phalaborwa’s annual production of separated neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide and 65% of its mixed SEG+ heavy rare earth carbonate. Pricing will be based on relevant rare earth indices under commercial terms. In exchange, Neo will provide technology, design input and technical support for Rainbow’s final solvent extraction circuit. Test work using material from Phalaborwa is underway at Neo’s facilities in Estonia and will be followed by an integrated pilot-scale campaign in Johannesburg. “We are delighted that Neo has agreed to partner with us,” Rainbow CEO George Bennett said. “Their deep understanding and experience in rare earth separation and magnet materials is invaluable.” The partnership resolves what Rainbow described as the remaining step needed to define its process for extracting rare earths from phosphogypsum waste. The company expects the PFS to establish its final products, processing route and waste streams with enough certainty to advance financing and permitting. items.headline: Researchers demonstrate random‑access quantum memory with seven cells
items.title: Random access quantum memory lets one processor select among seven storage cells
items.scifi_hook: A quantum chip can now pick data from any of seven storage spots instantly.
items.eli5: Scientists built a quantum memory that lets a processor retrieve information from chosen cells without scanning all.
items.why: Improves speed and flexibility of future quantum computers.
items.text: Classical computers can temporarily store the information required to perform specific tasks in a short-term memory component known as RAM (random access memory). This component allows computer processors to retrieve information from a chosen location without searching through all stored data.

items.headline: Qingxing raises ~100M yuan to build quantum‑inspired AI on GPUs
items.title: China’s Qingxing Raises Nearly 100 Million Yuan to Develop Quantum-Inspired AI
items.scifi_hook: A Chinese startup runs quantum‑style AI on ordinary graphics cards, matching big‑quantum models with far fewer parameters.
items.eli5: Qingxing uses regular GPU chips to mimic quantum computing tricks, getting 95% of a larger model's performance with ten‑times fewer settings.
items.why: It could make high‑performance AI cheaper and more accessible.
items.text: Insider Brief Qingxing Heterogeneous Computing completed a Series A+ funding round, bringing its total raised across two rounds in three months to nearly 100 million yuan (about $14.9 million) to develop quantum-inspired AI. Its RiverONE model runs on conventional GPUs and reportedly achieved at least 95% of a larger comparison model’s performance on a specialized quantum calibration task with less than one-tenth as many parameters. The company is working with chipmakers including Biren Technology and MetaX to adapt quantum software and AI models to their hardware, although the report did not disclose revenue from those partnerships. items.headline: India's DRDO partners with Zero mK India to build 20 mK quantum fridge
items.title: DRDO Partners With Zero mK India on 20 mK Quantum Refrigerator
items.scifi_hook: India's defense lab teams with a startup to create an ultra‑cold refrigerator that reaches just 20 millikelvin for quantum experiments.
items.eli5: A dilution refrigerator cools equipment to near absolute zero, enabling quantum computers and sensors to work.
items.why: It reduces reliance on imported cryogenic gear and boosts domestic quantum tech.
items.text: Insider Brief India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has signed a Technology Development Fund agreement with Zero mK India to develop an indigenous 20 mK dilution refrigerator for quantum applications. The project is the first high-value deep-tech agreement under the Technology Development Fund, which has a Rs 500 crore allocation approved for deep-tech and advanced technology projects. The refrigerator project is intended to strengthen India’s domestic capabilities in quantum technology and cryogenics while reducing reliance on imported cryogenic equipment. India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has entered its first high-value deep-tech project agreement under the Technology Development Fund scheme, partnering with start-up Zero mK India Private Limited to build an indigenous 20 mK dilution refrigerator for quantum applications, India Blooms reported . The agreement was signed in New Delhi by the Director of the Technology Development Fund and representatives from Zero mK India, a company based in Alwar, Rajasthan. It marks the first high-value deal drawn from the Rs 500 crore fund that Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved to back deep-tech and advanced technology projects. Dilution refrigerators are cryogenic systems built to reach extremely low temperatures in the millikelvin range, conditions that are necessary for operating and testing several quantum computing platforms and related quantum technologies.
